subject: geography
title: Impacts of Globalisation
meta_desc: A-Level Geography adventure on globalisation impacts, winners, losers and anti-globalisation.
final_note: Globalisation creates winners and losers within and between countries.

walkthroughs.body_html: China lifted 800 million out of poverty (1981-2018) via export-led growth. India IT sector employs 5 million in BPO and software. Consumer prices fell in MEDCs (Walmart effect). Transnational elite captured large share of gains: Oxfam (2023) says 1 percent took two-thirds of new wealth.

US Rust Belt manufacturing employment fell from 19 million (1979) to 12 million (2020). Detroit lost 60 percent of population since 1950. UK steel: Port Talbot blast furnaces closed 2024, losing 2800 jobs. Globalisation backlash drove Brexit and Trump political shifts.

Seattle 1999 WTO protests mobilised 40000 demonstrators against trade rules. Fair Trade certification covers 1.66 million producers across 70 countries. Slow Food movement (1986 Italy) celebrates local food. Localism and degrowth offer counter-narratives.

mcqs.q: What is the 'race to the bottom' critique of globalisation?
options: Glocalisation is a typo of globalisation.

The argument that TNCs play countries off against each other, relocating to those with lowest wages, weakest regulation and lowest taxes — pressuring governments to cut standards to attract investment.
The race to the bottom means TNCs compete with each other for the lowest prices.
Race to the bottom is when companies offshore work to mines and underground factories.
Glocalisation means the destruction of local cultures by global brands.
Glocalisation is a typo of globalisation.
Race to the bottom is when companies offshore work to mines and underground factories.
The adaptation of global products or services to local tastes, regulations or cultures — e.g. McDonald's offering paneer burgers in India or Tesco selling local foods in different countries.

mcqs.q: Why do TNCs locate production in LICs?
options: Because LICs have better infrastructure than HICs.
Because TNCs want to develop poorer countries and lift them out of poverty.
Lower labour costs, weaker regulation, access to raw materials, large potential markets, and government incentives like tax breaks in special economic zones.
Race to the bottom is when companies offshore work to mines and underground factories.
